Would anyone care to take a stab at explaining this to someone who scraped through most of his higher math classes with barely a C average?

He arranged the numbers in 12 slices, similar to a clock. This visually makes the numbers into base 12, instead of base 10. Let me go over number bases really quick. Think of what a number is representing. Say the number 784. Essentially this number is representing 7(10)^2 + 8(10)^1 + 4(10)^0 = 784. See the 10s with the powers lowering?

Binary is base 2, you know the 1s and 0s you always hear about. This means that in base 2, there can't be any more digits other than 0 and 1. So, if you take the binary number 110, it equals 1(2)^2 + 1(2)^1 + 0(2)^0 = 6 (in base 10). Tesla has organized that map in base 12.

He did this because 12 is a highly composite number — the smallest number with exactly four divisors: 2, 3, 4, and 6 (six if you count 1 and 12). 10 has only two. Consequently, 12 is much more practical when using fractions — it's easier to divide units of weights and measures into 12 parts, namely halves, thirds, and quarters — you already know how to do this, think of a clock, what's a half hour? 30 minutes. A quarter hour? 15 minutes. What is a third of an hour? 20 minutes. Now if you were in base 10, what is a third of 10? 3.33333333333333333333, you can see how this can be problematic.

By using base 12, easy to remember patterns emerge for the factors of 12, (2,3,4,and 6), where you will always return back to the "slice" you started in. Just so you know, he is counting by these numbers, like 3, 6, 9, 12, etc., so you just follow the path on his map. The prime numbers however create star patterns where you will never return to the column you were in. Some of these slices contain only prime numbers (with some exceptions, which all happen to be multiples of 5 and 7 or 11 and 13), and every prime number you square will end up in the 1'o'clock column (which is one of the columns which contain only prime numbers (with some exceptions as noted). The spiral patterns he included on the bottom right will help to identify the primes which are exceptions to the rule. If the number falls in the spiral path, its probably not prime (I don't know for sure about this because I don't have the time to prove it, but it seems fairly reasonable).

Thams for the great explanation.

Yes. The slices 1, 5, 7, and 11 will exclusively contain all of the prime numbers in existence greater than 3. Also, these prime numbers will have the last digit of either a 1, 5, or 7 (or Ɛ (which represents the number "11" if we are in base 12) which still technically ends in a 1).
